The space station, a monolithic structure of cold, unyielding alloy, hung in the silent void like a forgotten sentinel. Its metallic corridors, long and labyrinthine, were lined with conduits that pulsed with a faint, rhythmic luminescence, mimicking the heartbeat of a dormant beast. The air within was recycled to a sterile chill, carrying the faint, metallic tang of ozone and the distant, ever-present hum of life-support systems that had been running for decades without a single maintenance cycle. Dust motes, frozen in time, drifted lazily through the shafts of artificial light, settling on control panels that had not been touched since the last crew departed.

Outside the reinforced viewing ports, the desolate planet below was a sphere of bruised purples and grays, its surface scarred by ancient impacts and devoid of any sign of life. It was a world stripped bare, its atmosphere thin and toxic, leaving only the jagged peaks of mountains and the deep, dark trenches of its crust exposed to the vacuum. The ballet of asteroids that danced against the inky backdrop of space was not merely a visual spectacle but a testament to the chaotic history of this sector. These rocks, remnants of a shattered moon or a failed colony ship, moved in slow, gravitational waltzes, their surfaces pitted and blackened by eons of cosmic radiation. The silence of space was absolute, broken only by the internal machinery of the station, creating a profound sense of isolation. This was a place where time seemed to stretch and warp, where the past was etched into the metal and the future was as uncertain as the trajectory of the drifting debris. The station stood as a solitary witness to the decay of the planet below, a monument to human ambition in a universe that cared little for its existence.
